extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in patent law, policy-makers, and IP practitioners
extracted.subtask_short: identifying and responding to patent trolls
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, indicators, legal standards, causes, effects and defensive/policy responses relating to 'patent trolls' (non-practicing entities that enforce patents aggressively). The page summarizes how to identify such entities, the procedural and remedial legal standards that affect them, and practical/legislative responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: behaviors characterizing a 'patent troll'
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that does one or more of the following: purchases a patent (often from a bankrupt firm) and then sues another company claiming infringement; enforces patents against purported infringers without intending to manufacture the patented product or supply the patented service; enforces patents but has no manufacturing or research base; focuses solely on enforcing patent rights; or asserts patent infringement claims against non-copiers or against a large industry of non-copiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term is pejorative and definitions are contested; related labels include patent holding company (PHC), patent monetization entity (PME), patent assertion entity (PAE), and non-practicing entity (NPE). Whether an entity is called a 'troll' can depend on its conduct and public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-practicing entity (NPE) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: "A patent owner who does not manufacture or use the patented invention, but rather than abandoning the right to exclude, an NPE seeks to enforce its right through the negotiation of licenses and litigation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NPE is a neutral descriptive term; not all NPEs are necessarily 'trolls' in the pejorative sense—context and behavior matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad-faith infringement-threat indicators (Vermont Consumer Protection Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vermont's law indicates bad faith where threat letters show lack of specificity of the alleged infringement, settlement demands or damage claims that include excessive licensing fees, and unreasonably short deadlines for payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Vermont statute gives recipients of threat letters the right to counter-sue in state court; similar state statutes or enforcement actions (e.g., FTC settlement vs MPHJ) can impose penalties for deceptive or abusive demand-letter campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue limitation rule (TC Heartland v. Kraft Foods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent litigation cases must be heard in the state in which the defendant is incorporated, restricting plaintiffs' ability to 'shop around' for favorable plaintiff-friendly forums (e.g., Eastern District of Texas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Supreme Court rule changes strategic choices for filing venue and reduces forum-shopping that had benefitted many assertion entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review (IPR) as administrative validity check
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR (created under the America Invents Act) allows an executive agency (the PTAB) to review the validity of a patent as an alternative to court litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR provides a potentially faster, agency-level route to invalidate questionable patents; Supreme Court upheld the IPR process (Oil States). Organizations like Unified Patents file IPRs to reduce PAEs' effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney fee-shifting standard after Octane Fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Octane Fitness v. ICON, courts have an easier pathway to award attorney fees/costs for frivolous patent lawsuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowering the barrier to fee-shifting is a tool to deter frivolous or abusive litigation by assertion entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctive-relief standard (eBay v. MercExchange)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must apply a traditional, discretionary four‑factor equitable test (standard reasonableness test) rather than automatically granting injunctions for patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because permanent injunctions are no longer automatic, assertion entities lose leverage from the threat of injunctions—this limits a key strategic weapon for trolls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages standard: reasonable royalty versus lost profits
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful patent plaintiff is entitled at least to a reasonable royalty determined according to norms in the field; patent owners who actually make and sell the invention may also recover lost profits, a remedy typically unavailable to non-manufacturing assertion entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The type of damages available affects the economic leverage and expected recovery for plaintiffs and thus influences settlement dynamics with PAEs/NPEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause: high litigation costs encourage nuisance settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: High defense costs (historically cited as $1M+ before trial and $2.5M for a complete defense) make defendants likely to settle even non-meritorious suits to avoid cost and uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This economic asymmetry is a primary driver of plaintiff-friendly settlements and the business model of many assertion entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause: examination backlog and low patent quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination backlogs can give patent examiners insufficient time, favoring speedy issuance of weak, invalid, or overly broad patents, which facilitates later assertion by trolls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improving patent quality and examination resources reduces the availability of weak patents that PAEs exploit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk indicator: software and business-method patents are especially vulnerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Software patents (and business-method patents) are described as particularly prone to abuse because software is inherently conceptual and claim scope can be hard to define; statistics show software patents litigate at higher rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should treat such patents as higher risk for assertion and heightened scrutiny when clearing freedom-to-operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive tactic: design arounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Designing around asserted patent claims can cap the amount a patent troll can reasonably demand, because the alternative to paying a license is redesign cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence and cost of design-arounds constrain licensing demands and should be part of negotiating/defense strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive tactic: patent watch / monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should monitor issued patents and published patent applications to detect potentially relevant patents early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early detection enables earlier clearance, design-arounds, licensing, or challenges before product investment escalates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive tactic: clearance search (freedom-to-operate search)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform searches for patents or pending applications that cover important product features before development or market introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive clearance searches can reveal risks and lead to purchasing licenses, designing around, or challenging patents preemptively (example: Edison bought a prior patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive tactic: opposition proceedings / reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: In Europe, third parties may initiate opposition proceedings; in the U.S. there is reexamination (and IPR) to challenge patent validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative challenge routes can be more efficient than district-court litigation for invalidating overbroad patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive tactic: litigation to challenge patent validity or misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants can go on the offensive by finding prior art, arguing invalidity, non-infringement, or patent misuse; successful challenges can eliminate the asserted patent and deter future assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggressive defense may be costly but can permanently neutralize a troll's portfolio if prior art or other defenses prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive tactic: early settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Settling early often costs far less than full litigation and can be a pragmatic choice to limit expense and disruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh strategic value of fighting versus expected litigation cost and precedent risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive tactic: patent infringement insurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurance products are available to help protect companies from the cost of defending against infringement claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insurance can manage financial risk though coverage terms and costs vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive tactic: defensive patent aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregators purchase patents or rights to keep them out of the hands of assertion entities, then provide members with broad licenses in exchange for a fixed fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defensive aggregators reduce risk of acquisition by PAEs and can be cost-effective for member coalitions; they accounted for a meaningful share of brokered patent sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal remedy: action for unjustified threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions (Australia, UK, and other countries) allow legal action against those who make unjustified threats of patent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a threat is unjustifiable, courts may enjoin the conduct or award damages; in some jurisdictions the only defense is to commence and win infringement proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactic: bounties to find prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary bounties have been offered to the public to identify prior art or arguments that invalidate a patent (or other patents in a troll's portfolio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowdsourced prior-art hunts can be an effective, low-cost way to undermine a troll's asserted patents and business model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation: clearer patents and higher novelty/non-obviousness standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Government reports recommend policies to foster clearer patents with a high standard of novelty and non-obviousness, reduce disparity in litigation costs between patent owners and technology users, and increase the adaptability of the system to new technologies and business models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger examination standards, clearer claim drafting, and litigation-cost reforms are proposed levers to reduce abusive assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy lever: loser-pays (cost-shifting) reduces trolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdictions with 'loser pays' fee-shifting regimes (e.g., many European countries) see less patent-troll activity because plaintiffs risk paying defendants' fees if suit is unsuccessful; by contrast, the U.S. 'American rule' historically left each side to bear its own attorney fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifting fee-risk to unsuccessful plaintiffs is cited as an effective deterrent to frivolous or nuisance claims.
